title: Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System
why: Stage 1 is this paper's section 2 turned into four commands: read it for the happens-before relation itself, so `recv` becoming max(local, incoming) + 1 is a consequence you can derive rather than a rule you memorised.

title: Distributed Systems - Cambridge lecture notes
why: The clearest short treatment of everything the first ladder asks for: chapter 3 gives Lamport and vector clocks with worked diagrams, and chapter 4 gives the causal-broadcast delivery rule that stage 18's buffer has to implement exactly. Section 7.1 is later the shortest honest account of two-phase commit for stage 63 - one no aborts, commit needs every vote, and a dead coordinator leaves prepared participants stuck - and section 5.1's retry-plus-deduplication argument is the reasoning behind stage 69's table of seen message ids.

title: Distributed systems for fun and profit
why: Read chapters 2 and 3 before you start: they set up time, order and replication in the vocabulary the rest of this track uses, so quorums and causality are already familiar words by the time a stage demands them. Chapter 4 then introduces two-phase commit as the least fault-tolerant way to keep one copy, which is the framing stage 63 needs, and chapter 5 is the gentlest page anywhere on read repair and on gossip as replica synchronisation - stages 73 and 74 in prose before you write either.

title: Maelstrom - a workbench for distributed systems exercises
why: A second playground for the same primitives, with its own checker: building a broadcast or a counter node here is the cheapest way to see whether your mental model of message passing survives contact with a network that reorders and drops.

title: Virtual Time and Global States of Distributed Systems
why: The source for the vector-clock comparison stage 2 asks you to implement - strictly-less-than componentwise, incomparable means concurrent - and, in its second half, the consistent-cut argument that makes stage 17's snapshot meaningful.

title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store
why: One paper covers five of the primitives stages: section 4.2 is stage 3's version vectors and siblings, 4.3 is the ring, 4.5 is N/R/W, 4.6 is sloppy quorums and hinted handoff, and 4.7 is Merkle anti-entropy. It is also the source for two algorithm stages - 4.6's hint left on a stand-in replica and the read repair that writes the newest version back to exactly the replicas that answered stale are stage 73 entire, and 4.8.1's gossip, where each node picks a random peer every second and reconciles, is what stage 74 counts rounds of.

title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
why: Chapter 5 on leaderless replication is the readable version of the quorum arithmetic in stage 8, and chapter 9 on linearizability is worth having read before the cluster ladder tells you a read has to reflect a write that happened on another member. Chapter 9 is also the standard treatment of two-phase commit and its blocking coordinator for stage 63, and chapter 8's fencing-token figure - the lock service handing out increasing tokens, the storage refusing a write that carries an old one - is the exact mechanism stage 71 grades.

title: Logical Physical Clocks and Consistent Snapshotting in Globally Distributed Databases
why: The algorithm listing in section 4 is exactly what stage 4's `now` and `recv` must compute, including the case where the wall clock has gone backwards and the counter has to carry the causality instead.

title: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database
why: Section 3 is the other answer to the problem stage 4 poses and stage 51 stresses: bound the clock error and wait it out. Read it to see the cost of using real time for ordering, which is why your HLC does not. Stage 72 is the same trick without the atomic clocks - commit-wait pauses for the uncertainty interval rather than trusting the timestamp, exactly as your lease holder gives up early and your granter waits late.

title: Consistent Hashing and Random Trees
why: Section 4 defines the ring and proves the property stage 6 measures: adding one node to n moves about 1/(n+1) of the keys and no others, which is the claim the tester simulates against your ring.

title: A Name-Based Mapping Scheme for Rendezvous
why: The original HRW paper, and the reason stage 7 asks for `locate-k` as well as `locate`: the ordering by descending weight is the whole scheme, and it hands you a replica list for free where a ring needs extra rules.

title: Replication - Riak KV concepts
why: A production system's plain-English account of N, R and W and of what happens when a node is down - useful at stage 9, where the point is that a sloppy quorum accepts the write but is not a quorum, and again at stage 73, where the same hint is handed to a live replica and replayed when the owner comes back.

title: Bloom Filters by Example
why: An interactive page where you can watch bits get set and a false positive appear; ten minutes here before stage 10 saves you from the usual bug of hashing once and reusing the value.

title: Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors
why: Bloom's own four pages, which is where the error-rate formula the tester holds you to comes from - the suite checks your measured false-positive rate against (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k, so it helps to know what each letter means.

title: HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm
why: Figure 3 is the algorithm stage 11 grades: the harmonic mean, the alpha_m constant and the small-range correction. The tester checks your estimate against a 1.04/sqrt(m) envelope, which is this paper's own error bound.

title: HyperLogLog in Practice: Algorithmic Engineering of a State of the Art Cardinality Estimation Algorithm
why: Google's corrections to the original: 64-bit hashes instead of the large-range fix, empirical bias correction and a sparse representation. Reach for it if your stage 11 estimate is fine in the middle and wrong at the ends.

title: RFC 6962: Certificate Transparency
why: Section 2.1 specifies exactly the hashing this track pins - 0x00 before a leaf, 0x01 before an internal node - and explains the domain separation that makes it safe, so stage 12's root hash matches the tester's the first time.

title: Repair - Apache Cassandra
why: The Merkle-diff stage in production form: how a real store builds trees over token ranges and exchanges only the differing subtrees, which is the round-trip discipline stage 13 scores you on with its `compared` count. It is also why stage 73's `sync` is the only operation in that stage that guarantees convergence: read repair and hints are opportunistic, and full repair is the one that compares everything.

title: About CRDTs
why: The index of the field, with the state-based versus operation-based split stated plainly - worth ten minutes before stage 14 so you know which kind you are building when the tester asks for `state` and `merge`.

title: A comprehensive study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types
why: The catalogue these three stages are drawn from: G-Counter and PN-Counter in section 3, LWW-Register and OR-Set in section 3.3, RGA in section 4. Every specification here is a merge that is commutative, associative and idempotent, which is precisely what the tester replays permutations to check.

title: Conflict-free Replicated Data Types
why: The shorter SSS paper, which proves the thing the longer study assumes: monotone states joined by a least upper bound converge whatever order updates arrive in. Read it if you want to know why your merge is correct rather than just observed to pass.

title: CRDTs: The Hard Parts
why: A talk about sequence CRDTs specifically, which is the one stage 16 asks for: it shows why insertion needs a stable identifier for the element you are inserting after, and what goes wrong with the naive designs.

title: Distributed Snapshots: Determining Global States of Distributed Systems
why: The marker rule in section 3 is stage 17 in full: record your own state when you first see a marker, then record each incoming channel until its marker arrives. The conserved total the tester checks is this paper's section 5 argument.

title: Scaling your API with rate limiters
why: Why a token bucket is the shape you want - a steady rate plus a burst allowance - explained from the operator's side, which makes stage 19's `take` semantics obvious before you write them.

title: Rate Limiting, Cells, and GCRA
why: The careful comparison of the two buckets stage 19 implements, including the arithmetic that lets you keep a bucket as one timestamp instead of a level you have to tick - and why refilling by elapsed time, never by a timer, is what makes it testable.

title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter
why: The operational case for the primitives in stage 20: what a retry storm looks like, why a capped exponential delay is not enough on its own, and why every client adding randomness is what actually spreads the load.

title: Exponential Backoff And Jitter
why: The post that named "full jitter", which is the exact formula stage 20 grades - u * min(cap, base * 2^attempt) - with the simulations showing why it beats both no jitter and equal jitter.

title: SWIM: Scalable Weakly-consistent Infection-style Process Group Membership Protocol
why: Section 4.2 introduces the suspicion mechanism stage 20 models: a missed ack makes a member suspect, not dead, and only the timeout promotes it - which is why your `status` has three answers and not two. Section 4.1 is then stage 74: updates piggybacked on the failure detector's pings spread infection-style, and the analysis there is where the O(log n) rounds your message counter should show comes from.

title: The phi Accrual Failure Detector
why: Section 3 derives phi from the distribution of past heartbeat intervals, which is what stage 20's `phi` command must return: a suspicion level that rises with the silence, not a boolean someone else had to pick a timeout for.

title: Why gRPC gateway - etcd
why: The page that explains the exact wire format ladder B is written against, with curl examples showing keys and values base64-encoded in a JSON body - start here at stage 21 and keep it open through stage 23.

title: API reference - etcd
why: The generated message-by-message reference: every field of PutRequest, RangeRequest, TxnRequest, LeaseGrantRequest and WatchCreateRequest with its meaning. When a stage sends a field you have not implemented, this is the page that tells you what it is supposed to do.

title: etcd API - etcd
why: The prose companion to the reference, and the most useful single page of the node ladder: the response header and its revision, how a range end makes a prefix, what a txn compares, how a watch is created and cancelled, and what compaction does to old revisions.

title: ProtoJSON Format - Protocol Buffers
why: Explains the two rules that trip up every hand-written node: 64-bit integers are JSON strings, and a field at its default value may be omitted entirely - so "no count" and "count zero" are the same answer.

title: RFC 4648: The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings
why: Section 4 is the encoding every key and value crosses the wire in; read the padding rules once so a key whose length is not a multiple of three does not become a decoding bug you chase through three stages.

title: Data model - etcd
why: The page that defines the revision as a store-wide counter and distinguishes create_revision, mod_revision and version per key - the three numbers stage 26 reads history with and stage 27 hands back in prev_kv.

title: etcd API guarantees - etcd
why: States precisely what a client is owed: writes are linearizable, reads are linearizable unless you ask for serializable, and watch events for one key arrive in revision order without gaps. Stage 38 is this page turned into a test.

title: Maintenance - etcd
why: The operator's view of compaction, which is what stage 30 asks you to implement: history below the compacted revision is gone, reads of it fail rather than silently returning the latest value, and the current revision is unaffected.

title: Status Codes - gRPC
why: The numbers stage 34 checks are gRPC's, not HTTP's: 3 invalid argument, 5 not found, 8 resource exhausted, 11 out of range, 14 unavailable. One table, and it makes every error response in the suite predictable.

title: Leases: An Efficient Fault-Tolerant Mechanism for Distributed File Cache Consistency
why: The paper that introduced the lease, including the part stages 31, 32 and 72 make you live with: expiry may be late but must never be early, because the holder and the grantor do not share a clock. Stage 72 turns that into arithmetic - the holder stops serving at expires_at minus the clock error, the granter will not re-grant until expires_at plus it - and this is the argument for why both sides of that gap are needed.

title: RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1
why: Section 7 is the chunked transfer coding that the watch and keepalive streams are delivered over, and section 9 is the connection reuse the harness depends on - the two parts of HTTP you cannot fake your way past on this ladder.

title: Write-Ahead Log - Patterns of Distributed Systems
why: The shortest correct description of the mechanism stage 35 kills you for not having: append the record, flush it, then answer. Read it before you write a store that acknowledges from memory - and again before stage 65, where the same discipline decides the protocol: the prepare record is forced out before the vote is sent, so after a crash the log answers the question instead of the participant guessing.

title: Can Applications Recover from fsync Failures?
why: What happens after fsync returns an error, which most code treats as impossible: the dirty pages may already be gone. Read it once you pass stage 35 and want to know how much of your durability story is still an assumption.

title: The Raft Consensus Algorithm
why: The front door: a one-paragraph summary, the visualisation, and the list of existing implementations you can read side by side when your own election will not converge at stage 36 or stage 56. Drive the interactive diagram until you have watched a split vote resolve on the next timeout and a log entry replicate to a majority, which is the picture stage 57 asks you to write down.

title: Raft: Understandable Distributed Consensus
why: An animated walk through election and replication, including a leader failing and a new term starting - twenty minutes here makes stages 36 and 56 concrete before you read a line of the paper, and the replication half shows the follower whose log disagrees being walked backwards, which is the case stage 57 truncates on.

title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)
why: Figure 2 is the specification stages 36 and 56 are graded against, rule by rule. Section 5.2 is the one-vote-per-term election and the up-to-date-log check; 5.3 is the AppendEntries consistency check stage 57 implements, and its idempotence is why stage 53's duplicated messages are harmless; 5.4 is why stage 44's acknowledged write cannot be lost, and 5.4.2 is the Figure 8 scenario stage 58 is named for - a leader may only advance the commit index onto an entry of its own term. Section 7 is stage 59's snapshot, and section 6 is stage 60's joint consensus.

title: etcd-io/raft
why: The raft library the reference implementation actually runs, with the design the paper leaves out: raft as a pure state machine that emits messages, so the transport, the disk and the clock stay outside it. Read `raft.go` when your own replication turns into tangled callbacks, the `confchange` package when stage 60's joint configuration will not leave the joint phase, and the snapshot handling when stage 59 has to answer a follower asking for an index that was already compacted away.

title: Paxos Made Simple
why: The fourteen pages stage 61 implements. P1 through P2c are the promise-and-accept rules your acceptor obeys, including the one that catches everyone out: a proposer must propose the value of the highest-numbered proposal its promises reported, and its own only when none did. Read it beside Raft at stage 36 too, for the invariant they share - any two majorities intersect, so a value chosen by one is seen by the next.

title: High-Water Mark - Patterns of Distributed Systems
why: Names the line stages 37 and 44 live on: the highest log index known to be on a majority, and therefore the furthest a member may let a client see. Everything above it is written but not yet committed. Stage 58 is that line computed - sort the match indices, take the majority element, and then refuse to move onto it unless the entry is from the current term.

title: Generation Clock - Patterns of Distributed Systems
why: Why a term number only ever increases and why every message carries it: it is what makes stage 56 step down the instant it sees a higher term, and what lets the cluster in stage 45 recognise a returning old leader as stale rather than believing its log. Stage 71's fencing token is the same counter under another name, handed to the client instead of kept between peers.

title: raft.tla - the Raft specification in TLA+
why: Ongaro's own TLA+ spec, and the fastest way to get precise about the invariants stages 39, 44, 45 and 58 test - leader completeness and state-machine safety as formulas you can run TLC against rather than sentences you hope you implemented. The `AdvanceCommitIndex` action is stage 58's commitment rule in four lines, including the clause that refuses an entry whose term is not the leader's own.

title: Consistency Models - Jepsen
why: An interactive lattice of models with a page for each, including which of them survive a partition - the precise vocabulary for saying what your cluster promises in stages 38 and 54, instead of "strongly consistent".

title: Linearizability: A Correctness Condition for Concurrent Objects
why: The definition stage 54's checker implements: each operation takes effect at one instant inside its own call/return window, and the resulting sequential history must be legal. Section 2 is what you need; the rest is why it composes.

title: Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services
why: The proof behind stage 40: if the minority answered writes during a partition, the majority could not stay linearizable. Read section 3 and the refusal your node has to produce stops feeling like a limitation.

title: Please stop calling databases CP or AP
why: A short corrective to read alongside the CAP proof: the theorem's "available" is a far stronger claim than what stage 41's majority does when it keeps serving, and conflating the two will muddle how you describe your own system.

title: Failure modes - etcd
why: Catalogues what the reference does when a minority fails, a leader fails, or the whole cluster restarts - which is the behaviour stages 40, 43 and 50 were written against. Read it before you decide what your node should do without a quorum.

title: Jepsen: etcd and Consul
why: The analysis that found stale reads in an earlier etcd because a read served locally by an isolated leader looks fine and is not - the exact mistake stages 40 and 52 are built to catch in your implementation.

title: Consensus: Bridging Theory and Practice
why: The long version of Raft, and the only source that treats the hardest stages properly: chapter 3's section on committing entries from previous terms is stage 58's rule with the counterexample worked through, chapter 4 gives both the joint consensus and the single-server membership change stage 60 and the cluster stages 48 and 49 need, and chapter 5 is snapshotting, log compaction and how a far-behind follower is caught up by one - stage 59 and stages 46 to 47 at once.

title: Disaster recovery - etcd
why: How a snapshot is taken and what restoring it does to member identity and cluster id - background for stage 47's snapshot catch-up, and for what stage 50 expects every member to still have after a full restart.

title: etcd learner design - etcd
why: Why adding a voting member to a healthy cluster can break it, and how a non-voting learner that catches up first avoids that - the reasoning behind the "unhealthy cluster" refusals stage 48 has to keep re-offering its change through.

title: Runtime reconfiguration - etcd
why: The exact sequence stages 48 and 49 perform: member add first, then start the new node with --initial-cluster-state existing, and remove before shutdown - plus why the cluster refuses a change it considers unsafe.

title: Porcupine - a fast linearizability checker in Go
why: The implementation this track's own checker is shaped after; read the model interface and the memoisation in `checker.go` to see the two optimisations that make the search finish on histories of real size.

title: Testing and Verifying Concurrent Objects
why: The original linearizability search - take a minimal operation, try it against the model, recurse, backtrack - which is the algorithm stage 54's checker runs over your history. Read it to understand why an operation whose response was lost has to be treated as optional.

title: Testing for Linearizability
why: Lowe's comparison of linearizability-testing algorithms, including the Wing and Gong search with memoisation that makes it tractable - the reference for why stage 54 can check a history of hundreds of operations at all.

title: Jepsen: etcd 3.4.3
why: The most recent full analysis of the exact system this ladder is validated against: which faults were injected, which anomalies turned up, and how a suspected lost update was traced. It is the closest thing to a worked answer for stages 54 and 55.

title: etcd robustness tests
why: etcd's own version of stages 54 and 55: randomized traffic, a failpoint-driven fault schedule and a linearizability check of the resulting history. Read the `traffic` and `validate` packages for what a mature version of your own harness looks like.

title: Elle - a transactional consistency checker
why: The other half of Jepsen's checking story: instead of searching for a linearization, Elle infers a dependency graph and looks for cycles, which scales to histories where stage 54's search would not finish. Worth knowing once stage 55 makes you want longer runs.

title: Implementing Replicated Logs with Paxos
why: Ousterhout and Ongaro's lecture deck, drawn one slide per message exchange. It is the cheapest way to get single-decree Paxos straight before stage 61, and the second half - one leader, phase one run once, phase two per slot - is exactly the move stage 62 is asking you to make.

title: Paxos Made Moderately Complex
why: Van Renesse and Altinbuken give multi-decree Paxos as pseudocode guided by its invariants, which is what stage 62 needs and what Paxos Made Simple deliberately withholds. The ballot/slot split, the rule that a higher ballot strips leadership without un-choosing a settled slot, and the contiguous-prefix requirement on the state machine are all here in a form you can transcribe.

title: Paxos Made Live - An Engineering Perspective
why: Chubby's authors on what stage 62's stable leader costs in practice: why they run with a master lease, what happens to throughput when two proposers duel over ballots, and the gap between the algorithm on paper and a system that has to survive disk faults and restarts. Read it after your multi-Paxos passes, for the list of things the tests do not model.

title: Two Phase Commit - Patterns of Distributed Systems
why: The pattern with working code either side of it: the coordinator collecting votes for stage 63, and - the part most write-ups skip - what each side has to have written down before it answers, which is the whole of stage 65. Start here, then read a paper.

title: Consensus on Transaction Commit
why: Section 2 is stage 63's participant as a four-state machine - working, prepared, committed, aborted - with the promise made explicit: once prepared, a participant may not decide for itself. It also states the Non-Blocking condition precisely, which is the property stage 64's extra phase is bought to obtain, and then shows that 2PC is Paxos Commit with a single acceptor, which is why one coordinator failure blocks it.

title: Nonblocking Commit Protocols
why: The paper that introduced three-phase commit and proved what the extra round buys: a protocol is nonblocking exactly when no reachable state is both committable and abortable, which is why the pre-commit state has to exist. It is also honest about the assumption stage 64 then breaks - the timeout rule reads 'no pre-commit arrived' as 'none was sent', which is only true without partitions.

title: PREPARE TRANSACTION - PostgreSQL
why: Stage 65 in a real database: PREPARE forces the transaction's state to disk and dissociates it from the session, so a crash leaves it listed in pg_prepared_xacts waiting to be told the decision. The warnings on this page - a prepared transaction holds its locks until someone resolves it - are why a participant with a prepare record and no decision must ask rather than choose.

title: Sagas
why: Garcia-Molina and Salem's original: a saga is a sequence T1..Tn where each Ti has a compensating Ci, and a failure at step k runs C(k-1)..C1 in reverse - stage 66's undo order, stated once and proved. Read section 3 for the requirement that compensations must be idempotent and must not fail permanently, which is why stage 66 retries a compensation until it succeeds.

title: Pattern: Saga
why: Richardson's write-up is the one that puts the two coordination styles side by side, which is the difference between stages 66 and 67: an orchestrator that remembers the completed steps and drives the undo, versus services that each react to one event and emit the next with no one holding the state. Read the trade-off list before you decide which failure is easier to debug.

title: Saga distributed transactions pattern
why: The most careful modern treatment of the two shapes, with the failure diagrams drawn. It names the properties stage 67 tests you on and stage 66 does not need: events are at-least-once, so a handler that has already run must emit nothing, and a chain already unwinding must absorb a second failure rather than start a second chain.

title: Pattern: Transactional outbox
why: States stage 68's problem in one line - you cannot atomically update a database and publish to a broker - and its answer: insert the event into an OUTBOX table in the same transaction as the row, and let something else publish it afterwards. Read it first, because the stage's naive case is exactly the dual write this rules out.

title: Reliable Microservices Data Exchange With the Outbox Pattern
why: The outbox with a real relay behind it, including the part stage 68 grades: the relay crashing between publishing and marking the record done leaves the record, so the event is sent again. This post is blunt that the outbox buys at-least-once and nothing more, which is the handoff to stage 69.

title: Pattern: Idempotent Consumer
why: The shape stage 69 implements: record the message id in the same transaction as the effect, and check it before applying rather than after. It also raises the question the stage turns into a test - how long you keep the ids, and what exactly-once means once the table has forgotten one.

title: Idempotent Receiver - Patterns of Distributed Systems
why: The pattern with both halves stage 69 needs: a per-client request id stored with the saved response, so a retransmission is answered from the record instead of applied twice, and an explicit discussion of expiring those records - which is the eviction policy the stage makes you get right. The saved-response half is also stage 70 before the HTTP vocabulary is put on it.

title: Idempotent requests - Stripe API
why: The reference definition of the header stage 70 implements, and short enough to read twice. Note the two rules the stage tests: the stored response is replayed for a repeated key, and reusing a key with a different request body is an error rather than a new charge.

title: Implementing Stripe-like Idempotency Keys in Postgres
why: The implementation behind the header, by someone who built it: keys are rows with a state, an in-flight key locks rather than races, and the work is split into atomic phases so a crash resumes from a recovery point. Stage 70's rule that a second request under a running key is refused rather than queued comes straight from here.

title: How to do distributed locking
why: The argument stage 71 is built on, with the figure to match: a client checks that it holds the lock, is paused by GC after the check, and writes after its lease has expired - so the lock service must hand out a monotonically increasing token and the resource must refuse anything below the highest it has seen. Read it for why checking `holder` first proves nothing.

title: Distributed locks with Redis - the Redlock algorithm
why: The algorithm the fencing argument is aimed at: acquire on a majority of independent Redis instances, each with a TTL, and treat the lock as held if enough of them answered within the validity time. Read it before the critiques so stage 71's question - what the resource does when a lock holder it believes in has already been superseded - has a concrete target.

title: Is Redlock safe?
why: Redis's author answering the fencing-token critique point by point. Read it beside Kleppmann's post at stage 71: the disagreement is about whether a lock can be made safe by timing alone, and the concession - that a mutual-exclusion guarantee at the resource needs a token the resource checks - is the reason the stage grades the fence and not the lock.

title: Lease - Patterns of Distributed Systems
why: The short version of what stage 72 implements: a lease is a lock with an expiry, renewal extends it from now rather than from the old deadline, and the holder has to give up before the granter believes it has. Read it first, then Gray and Cheriton for why the two clocks make that gap mandatory.

title: Hints - Apache Cassandra
why: Hinted handoff as an operator sees it: where the hint is stored, when it is replayed, and - the part stage 73 turns into a test - that a hint is not a guarantee. Hints have a window and they die with the node holding them, which is why the stage's `sync` compares everything rather than trusting that the hints were delivered.

title: Gossiping in Distributed Systems
why: A twelve-page survey that gives stage 74 its arithmetic: the anti-entropy and rumour-mongering models, what fanout does to the number of rounds, and why an epidemic reaches every node in O(log n) rounds while the message count keeps climbing. Read it to know what your round-by-round counts should look like before you trust them.

title: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software
why: The book that named both patterns. The stability chapters are where the circuit breaker of stage 75 comes from - a breaker exists so a caller stops spending threads on a dependency that is already failing - and the bulkhead of stage 77, where partitioning resources means one saturated pool cannot take the whole process with it. Read the antipattern chapters first: they are the failures the stages simulate.

title: CircuitBreaker
why: Six hundred words and a state diagram covering all three states stage 75 implements: closed with a failure counter, open with a reset timeout, and the half-open trial whose single result decides which way the breaker goes. Read the note on what counts as a failure before you decide whether a call rejected while open is evidence about the dependency.

title: Addressing Cascading Failures - Google SRE Book
why: Why stages 75 and 77 exist. The chapter walks a server into overload and shows the feedback loops that keep it there - unbounded queues turning latency into timeouts, retries multiplying the load, one slow dependency consuming every thread - and then names the ways out, which are the breaker, the bounded pool and the shed request you are about to implement.

title: The Tail at Scale
why: Dean and Barroso's paper is where stage 76's technique is named and measured: send the hedge only after the primary has passed a high percentile, so the extra load is a percent or two, and cancel the loser the moment either answers. The 95th-percentile trigger and the resulting p99 numbers are the reason the stage refuses to hedge below its threshold.

title: gRPC request hedging
why: Hedging as a configuration knob: hedgingDelay is stage 76's hedge_after_ms, maxAttempts caps how many copies exist, and the first non-failing response wins while the rest are cancelled. Useful at stage 76 for seeing that the rule you are implementing is a real, shipped policy and not a thought experiment.

title: Handling Overload - Google SRE Book
why: The chapter stage 77 is modelled on: rejecting work cheaply is better than accepting it and being too slow to finish, a request whose deadline has already passed is free to drop, and per-client quotas keep one caller from consuming the capacity of the rest. It is also the source of the stage's distinction between shedding stale work and rejecting a caller.

title: Using load shedding to avoid overload
why: The operational half of stage 77, with graphs: what a service's throughput curve does past its limit, why an unbounded queue is how one slow dependency takes everything, and why the limit should be on concurrency rather than on the queue. Read the section on dropping work whose deadline has passed - the stage counts that as capacity recovered, not as a rejection.

title: Strong consistency models (Aphyr)
why: The map of the territory, drawn as a lattice from linearizable down to eventual, with what each model forbids and what it costs. Read this before the papers: it is the piece that makes the hierarchy make sense rather than being a list of names.

title: Consistency (Princeton COS 418 lecture notes)
why: Worked examples of histories that are sequential but not linearizable, and the quorum arithmetic behind a replicated register. The diagrams are the fastest way to see why real time is the only difference between the two models stage 78 checks.

title: Highly Available Transactions: Virtues and Limitations
why: Maps out exactly which guarantees a system can offer while staying available under partition, and the session guarantees sit right on that line — read-your-writes and monotonic reads are achievable, linearizability is not. Section 4 is the one to read for stage 79.

title: Chain Replication for Supporting High Throughput and Availability
why: The paper stage 81 is built from. Section 2 gives the prefix invariant in two sentences and section 3 works through each of the three failure positions — head, tail and middle — which is the part most summaries leave out.

title: Consistent Core (Patterns of Distributed Systems)
why: Why a system usually runs a small consensus cluster beside a large data cluster rather than putting everything through consensus — the practical framing for why stage 80's consensus-free register and stage 82's ReadIndex both exist.

title: Introduction to Reliable and Secure Distributed Programming
why: The book these three stages come from. It builds every abstraction as a module with stated properties and an algorithm that implements it — best-effort to uniform broadcast, then the ordering layers, then the detector classes — which is exactly the shape of section O.

title: Failure detectors (Aspnes, Yale CS notes)
why: The classes on one page: the completeness/accuracy grid, why ◇W and ◇S are equivalent, and a sketch of the reduction showing ◇S is the weakest class that solves consensus — the Chandra–Toueg result, without the paywall the paper itself sits behind.

title: Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (Castro and Liskov)
why: Where the 3f + 1 sizing stops being arithmetic and becomes a protocol. Section 4 shows the three-phase message pattern the quorum bound forces, and why two rounds are needed where a crash-fault protocol manages with one.

title: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database
why: Section 3 is the TrueTime API — an interval, not an instant — and section 4.1.2 is commit-wait in a page. The rest of the paper is what becomes possible once a database can compare timestamps across continents.

title: Large-scale Incremental Processing Using Distributed Transactions and Notifications
why: Percolator: snapshot isolation built on a key/value store with nothing but timestamps, locks and two-phase commit. Section 2.2 is the algorithm stage 88 implements, including the primary lock that makes a crashed client's transaction recoverable.

title: Percolator, walked through (TiKV deep dive)
why: The same algorithm with diagrams of the lock and write columns at each step, from a database that actually implements it. Read this first and the paper second.

title: Linearizability versus Serializability (Bailis)
why: Two words used interchangeably and meaning different things: one is about single objects and real time, the other about transactions and equivalence to some serial order. Stage 78 checks the first and stage 88 the second, and this is the page that keeps them apart.
